intro: A broader pull this week thanks to a filter fix — GitHub and Hacker News finally show up alongside Product Hunt, and the result reads less like a product showcase and more like a status report on what happens once agents get real autonomy. A Copilot-assisted PR became the entry point for an actual compromise at Snowflake. Claude Code got a silent server-side change to how hard it tries, no client update required. And two tools showed up on opposite ends of the accountability spectrum: one puts a team review gate in front of what an agent ships, another quietly defeats the automation-detection your security tooling probably assumes still works. Progress, mostly — read the fine print.

items.title: FetchSandbox MCP
items.note: FetchSandbox MCP targets a specific failure mode this audience will recognize: an agent's fix passes CI while the underlying data or integration behavior is still wrong. It reproduces the real failure against one of 70+ API sandboxes and re-verifies the fix actually held, rather than trusting a green test run — positioned explicitly as "a receipt, not a vibe." For a team that has to show its work on why an AI-assisted change was safe to ship, that's the right instinct, though the excerpt doesn't say what the receipt actually contains or where it's stored for later audit.

claims.supported_by: Your agent's integration fix passes CI. The data is still wrong.

items.title: Anthropic appears to be A/B testing reduced effort levels in Claude Code
items.note: An HN commenter reports Anthropic silently enrolling some Claude Code sessions (Fable 5, version 2.1.236+) into a server-side experiment that shrinks the effort scale — no client update required to trigger it, with older versions and Opus 5 sessions left alone. The report itself frames this as probably an A/B test, not a confirmed universal rollout, and there's no official Anthropic statement cited here. Still worth flagging: a coding agent's reasoning behavior changing server-side and invisibly, mid-deployment, is exactly the kind of vendor-controlled variable that's hard to account for in a change-managed environment.

items.title: AI-Generated GitHub Copilot “Autofix” Allowed Compromise of Snowflake's Jira
items.note: Security researchers at Wiz report their Red Agent found its way into Snowflake's internal Jira through a flaw introduced via a GitHub Copilot-assisted pull request — a concrete example of an AI-assisted code change becoming the entry point for a real compromise chain, not a hypothetical one. The excerpt here is a one-line summary, not the full writeup, so it's worth reading the source directly before drawing conclusions about what specifically went wrong in review.

claims.text: Wiz's Red Agent found its way into Snowflake's internal Jira
claims.supported_by: Wiz Red Agent finds its way into Snowflake's internal Jira

claims.text: The entry point was a flaw introduced through a GitHub Copilot-assisted pull request
claims.supported_by: through a flaw in a GitHub Copilot–Assisted PR

items.hook: A real security compromise that started with an AI-assisted pull request, not a hypothetical one.

items.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
items.note: Proliferate is an open-source IDE layer for running Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and other coding agents in parallel, locally or in the cloud, with reusable workflows. Running it locally is the operative option for this audience: keeping the orchestration layer on infrastructure you control, rather than a vendor's, is the same architectural answer this list keeps seeing to the "can we actually adopt this" question — not a compliance feature bolted on, but a deployment model that avoids the question in the first place.

items.title: Coding Agents killed my identity. How do you feel?
items.note: A full-time software engineer writes on HN that they realized they hadn't personally written code in over a month — not from moving into management, but because agents had gradually taken over first the boilerplate, then the planning and architecture, leaving them mostly supplying context and infrastructure details. Framed as "winning with a chess engine": still shipping, but with the part of the job they valued removed. Worth surfacing for any engineering lead rolling out agent adoption — retention and job-satisfaction risk is a real cost that a pure productivity metric won't show.

claims.supported_by: Half a year ago I suddenly realized I hadn't written any code for over a month, and I am a full-time software dev without any managing work

items.title: Slack Code
items.note: Slack Code puts an agent's work inside a dedicated, shared Slack channel where the team watches it work, reviews diffs, and explicitly approves what ships — turning what's usually a solo, unreviewed agent session into something with a visible team approval step. For a regulated team, "who approved this AI-generated change and where's the record" is exactly the kind of question this starts to answer, though the excerpt doesn't say whether that approval trail is retained anywhere durable, or just lives in Slack's normal message history.

claims.text: Slack Code creates a dedicated code channel when a coding agent is mentioned, where teammates plan, watch the agent work, review diffs, test live previews, give feedback, and approve what ships
claims.supported_by: Slack Code turns coding with AI from a solo session into a team sport. Mention a coding agent and Slack creates a dedicated code channel where teammates can plan together, watch the agent work, review code diffs, test live previews, give feedback, and approve what ships.

claims.text: It supports agents including Claude, Devin, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and Vercel agents
claims.supported_by: Bring Claude, Devin, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Vercel agents, and your team into the same place

items.title: Show HN: Hands-Rust MCP/CLI that sees the Windows desktop and clicks real Chrome
items.note: Hands is a Rust MCP/CLI that lets a coding-agent harness (Grok, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, etc.) drive a real Chrome profile via actual OS-level input — not Playwright, Puppeteer, or a remote debugging port — specifically so sites that key off CDP/automation flags mostly don't detect it as automated. Genuinely useful for legitimate testing, and also a direct description of how to make agent-driven browser activity indistinguishable from a human's to any system trying to tell the difference. Worth knowing this class of tool exists before assuming your bot-detection or session-monitoring controls would catch an unsanctioned agent using one.

claims.text: Hands drives Chrome via OS SendInput clicks on a real profile, not a Chrome DevTools click
claims.supported_by: Click is OS SendInput on a Bézier path, not a Chrome DevTools click.
